headline: Lewiston Memorial Bill Clears Committee Unanimously, Heads to Full Legislature
body:
AUGUSTA — A bill to establish a permanent state memorial at the site of the 2023 Lewiston shooting passed unanimously out of the Joint Committee on Veterans and Legal Affairs on Tuesday, clearing the way for a full vote in the Maine Legislature next week.

The bill, LD 2041, sponsored by Sen. Peggy Rotundo (D-Lewiston), would allocate $500,000 for the construction of a memorial and mental health resource center at the site where eighteen people were killed and thirteen others wounded in October 2023.

The committee vote was 13-0, with no members abstaining. The legislation now heads to the full Senate and House, where leadership in both parties has indicated it will pass.

"Today, the committee sent a clear message: we will not forget what happened in Lewiston, and we will build something worthy of those we lost," Rotundo said after the vote.

Families of the victims testified before the committee earlier this month. Ben Dyer, whose sister Tricia Asselin was killed, urged lawmakers to look beyond partisan politics.

"This isn't about politics," Dyer said. "It's about making sure we never forget what happened, and that we give people a place to heal."

The memorial would be built on the site of the former Schemengees Bar and Grille and Just-In-Time Recreation, the two locations where the shooting occurred. The mental health resource center would provide counseling services and support groups for survivors, first responders, and community members.

Committee members from both parties praised the bill's approach. Sen. Richard Bradstreet (R-Kennebec), a member of the committee, called it "a bill that should never have been necessary, but one we have a duty to pass."

The $500,000 appropriation would come from the state's general fund. Some Republican lawmakers have raised concerns about spending amid broader budget negotiations, but none voted against the bill in committee.

The full Legislature is scheduled to vote on LD 2041 on August 26.

The 2023 shooting was the deadliest mass shooting in Maine history. A report issued by an independent commission earlier this year found that law enforcement had "sufficient probable cause" to take the shooter into protective custody prior to the attack, and that missed opportunities to intervene contributed to the tragedy.

The shooter, Robert Card, was found dead of a self-inflicted gunshot wound two days after the shooting.

Since then, the Maine Legislature has passed several gun safety measures, including expanded background checks and a "yellow flag" law allowing law enforcement to temporarily remove firearms from individuals in crisis. The memorial bill is the first legislative effort to create a permanent physical marker of the event.

"This memorial won't bring anyone back," Rotundo said. "But it will ensure that the people of Lewiston — and the people of Maine — have a place to gather, to remember, and to heal."
